Behind the scenes

How the AI satellites handled it

Each satellite got its own AI agent. They argued in plain English about who should move. Every deal went to a physics referee that checks fuel and re-runs the orbits. A deal that doesn't actually clear doesn't count, however good the argument sounds.

    More close calls

    About Close Call

    Thousands of working satellites share low Earth orbit with tens of thousands of pieces of tracked debris. Close approaches are predicted every day, and there's no air-traffic control up there. When two operators' satellites are on course for a near-miss, they usually work it out by email. That's how it went in September 2019, when ESA moved its Aeolus satellite out of a Starlink's way.

    What you're doing

    Each daily puzzle starts from a real predicted close approach published by CelesTrak SOCRATES. You fire one short burn of the thrusters. Fire earlier and a small push has time to grow into a big change of course. Fire late and you need a lot more fuel. For a satellite, fuel is lifespan.

    How it's judged

    A real orbital-mechanics engine runs in your browser and checks your burn. It works out where both objects will be, how close they'll pass, whether you had the fuel, and whether your new path runs into anything else. "Safe" means more than 5 km apart. Your score compares your fuel with the cheapest dodge the solver could find.

    The AI part

    The same encounter is handed to AI agents, one per satellite. They negotiate who should move, under the same referee. Sometimes they find a good deal. Often they burn far later, and far more expensively, than they needed to. That gap is why this exists: automated coordination needs a judge that checks the physics, not just the argument.

    Honesty notes

    The objects, names, and predicted encounter times come from real data. We start our own simplified model (two-body orbits) ten minutes before the encounter, so our miss distance differs from the official prediction. Fuel budgets and right-of-way are assumptions, because operators don't publish them. This is a teaching game, not operational advice.
